place.e: From Middle English place, conflation of Old English plæċe (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French place (“place, an open space”), both from Latin platēa (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”).
place.g: An area; somewhere within an area.

place.e: From Middle English placen, from the noun (see above).
place.g: To put (someone or something) in a specific location.

plague.e: From Middle English plage, borrowed from Old French plage, from Latin plāga (“blow, wound”), from plangō (“to strike”). Middle Low German plāge; Middle High German plāge, pflāge (> German Plage); plāgen (> German plagen); Swedish plåga; French plaie, Occitan plaga.
plague.g: The bubonic plague, the pestilent disease caused by the virulent bacterium Yersinia pestis.

plain.e: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pleyn, playn, Middle French plain, plein, and Old French plain, from Latin plānus (“flat, even, level, plain”).
From Old French plain, from Latin plānum (“level ground, a plain”), neuter substantive from plānus (“level, even, flat”).
plain.g: An expanse of land with relatively low relief and few trees, especially a grassy expanse.

plainly.e: From Middle English playnly, pleinly, pleyneliche, equivalent to plain + -ly.
plainly.g: In a plain manner; simply; basically.

plait.e: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ (plestí) and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced.
plait.g: A flat fold; a doubling, as of cloth; a pleat.

plan.e: Borrowed from French plan (“flat surface, ground plot, map”), from Latin plānus. Some sources also argue for influence or alteration of French plant, from plantar, from Latin plantāre (“set, fix in place”).
plan.g: A drawing showing technical details of a building, machine, etc., with unwanted details omitted, and often using symbols rather than detaile

plane.e: From Latin plānum (“flat surface”), a noun use of the neuter of plānus (“plain”). The word was introduced in the 17th century to distinguish the geometrical senses from the other senses of plain.
plane.g: Of a surface: flat or level.

plane.e: From Middle English plane, plaine, from Anglo-Norman plaine, from Late Latin plāna (“planing tool”).
plane.g: A tool for smoothing wood by removing thin layers from the surface.

planet.e: From Middle English planete, from Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”) (itself an ellipsis of ἀστέρες πλανῆται (astéres planêtai, “wandering stars”)), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin.
planet.g: Each of the seven major bodies which move relative to the fixed stars in the night sky—the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and

plank.e: From Middle English plank, planke, borrowed from Old French planke, Old Northern French planque (compare French planche, from Old French planche), from Vulgar Latin planca, from palanca, from Latin phalanga. The Latin term derives from the Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), so it is thus a doublet of phalange and phalanx.
plank.g: A long, broad and thick piece of timber, as opposed to a board which is less thick.

plant.e: From Middle English plante, from Old English plante (“young tree or shrub, herb newly planted”), from Proto-West Germanic *plantu, from Latin planta (“sprout, shoot, cutting”). Broader sense of "any vegetable life, vegetation generally" is from Old French plante.
plant.g: An organism that is not an animal, especially an organism capable of photosynthesis, and typically a small or herbaceous organism of this ki

plantation.e: Borrowed from Middle French plantation, from Latin plantātiō (“planting, transplanting”), from plantātus (“planted”), the perfect passive participle of plantāre, + action noun suffix -tiō.
plantation.g: A large farm; estate or area of land designated for agricultural growth. Often includes housing for the owner and workers.

plaster.e: From Middle English plaster, plastre, from Old English plaster, from late Latin plastrum, shortened from Classical Latin emplastrum (“a plaster, bandage”); later reinforced by Anglo-Norman plastre.
plaster.g: A paste applied to the skin for healing or cosmetic purposes.

plat.e: From Middle English plat, plate, platte (“flat; smooth; blunt, plain”), from Anglo-Norman, Middle French, and Old French plat (“(adjective) flat, level; calm; blunt, plain; (adverb) in a flat position; directly, straight; bluntly, plainly”), from Vulgar Latin *plattus (“flat; smooth”).
plat.g: Flat; level; (by extension) frank, on the level.

plate.e: From Middle English plate, from Old French plate, from Medieval Latin plata, from Vulgar Latin *plat(t)us, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat, wide”).
plate.g: A slightly curved but almost flat dish from which food is served or eaten.
Silver or gold, in the form of a coin, or less often silver or gold utensils or dishes.

plateau.e: Borrowed from French plateau, diminutive of plat (“a plate”); see plate.
plateau.g: A largely level expanse of land at a high elevation; tableland.

platform.e: From Middle French plateforme (“a flat form”), from plate (“flat”) (from Old French plat, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “flat”)) + forme (“form”) (from Latin fōrma (“shape; figure; form”)); compare flatscape.
platform.g: A raised stage from which speeches are made and on which musical and other performances are made.

plating.e: From Middle English *platynge, from Old English platung (“plate, thin piece of metal”), equivalent to plate + -ing.
plating.g: An act of determining where a postage stamp is positioned on a sheet.

platter.e: From Middle English plater, from Anglo-Norman plater, dissimilatory variant of platel, from Old French plate (“metal plate”) (see plate).

play.e: From Middle English pleyen (verb) and Middle English pleye (noun), from Old English plegian and plegan, plagian (“to play, exercise, etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *plehan (“to care about, be concerned with”) and Proto-West Germanic *plegōn (“to engage, move”), of uncertain origin.
play.g: To act in a manner such that one has fun; to engage in activities expressly for the purpose of recreation or entertainment.

player.e: From Middle English pleyere, pleyer, from Old English pleġere (“player, athlete, wrestler”), from Proto-West Germanic *plegārī. Equivalent to play + -er.

playing.e: From Middle English playing; equivalent to play + -ing.
playing.g: An occasion on which something, such as a song or show, is played.

plaza.e: Borrowed from Spanish plaza (“town-square or central place of gathering”), from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), clipping of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”).

plea.e: From Middle English ple, from Old French plait, plaid, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc., Latin an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placere (“to please”).
plea.g: An appeal, petition, urgent prayer or entreaty.

plead.e: From Middle English pleden, plaiden, from Old French plaider (“to plead, offer a plea”), from plait, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc.", in Classical Latin, "an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placeō (“to please”).
plead.g: To present (an argument or a plea), especially in a legal case.

pleading.g: The act of making a plea.

pleasant.e: From Middle English plesaunte, from Old French plaisant. By surface analysis, please + -ant. Partly displaced Old English wynsum, which became Modern English winsome.

please.e: From Middle English plesen, plaisen, borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native Old English līcian, whence Modern English like.
please.g: To make happy or satisfy; to give pleasure to.

please.e: Short for if you please, an intransitive, ergative form taken from if it please you which is a calque of French s'il vous plaît, which replaced pray. If it please you is a present subjunctive form, but most current uses of please are not parsed that way.
please.g: Used to make a polite request.

pleased.e: From Middle English plesed, iplesed (past participle) and Middle English plesede (preterit), both equivalent to please + -ed.

pleasing.e: From Middle English plesynge, pleizinge, plesende (present participle), equivalent to please + -ing.
pleasing.g: Agreeable; giving pleasure, cheer, enjoyment or gratification.

pleasure.e: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-k- (“wide and flat”).
pleasure.g: A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.

pledge.e: From Middle English plege, from Anglo-Norman plege, from Old French plege (Modern French pleige) from Medieval Latin plevium, plebium, from plebiō (“to pledge”), from Frankish *plehan (“to pledge; to support; to guarantee”).
pledge.g: To make a solemn promise (to do something).

plenteous.e: From Middle English plentewos, plentevous, et al., circa 1300, from Old French plentiveus (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from plentif (“abundant”), from plenté (“abundance”) (Modern French pleinté, English plenty), from Latin plenitatem, accusative of plenitas (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

plentiful.e: From Middle English plentiful, plentyfull, plentefull, equivalent to plenty + -ful.
plentiful.g: Existing in large number or ample amount.

plentifully.e: From Middle English plentefully, plentefullych, plentyfullyche, equivalent to plentiful + -ly.

plenty.e: From Anglo-Norman plent(é) + -y, from Middle English plentie, plentee, plente, from Anglo-Norman plenté, from Old French plenté, from Latin plēnitātem, accusative of plēnitās (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), from which English full also comes, via Proto-Germanic.
plenty.g: A more-than-adequate amount; plenitude; a great deal.

plight.e: From Middle English plit (“fold, wrinkle, bad situation”), conflation of Middle English pliht, plight (“risky promise, peril”) (from Old English pliht "danger, risk"; see Etymology 2) and Anglo-Norman plit, plyte (“fold, condition”), from Old French pleit (“condition, manner of folding”) (from Vulgar Latin *plictum, from Latin plicitum (“fold”)).

From Middle English plight (“risk, danger”), from Old English pliht (“peril, risk, danger, damage, plight”), from Proto-West Germanic *plihti (“care, responsibility, duty”). A suffixed form of the root represented by Old English pleoh (“risk, danger, hurt, peril"; also "responsibility”) and plēon (“to endanger, risk”).
plight.g: Responsibility for ensuing consequences; risk; danger; peril.

plot.e: From Middle English plot, plotte, from late Old English plot (“a plot of ground”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *plataz, *platjaz (“a patch”); or alternatively, perhaps from a rebracketing of Old English land-splott (“small portion, or plot, of ground”) taken as landes-plot (“plot of land”).
plot.g: The course of a story, comprising a series of incidents which are gradually unfolded, sometimes by unexpected means.

plough.e: From Middle English plouh, plow, plugh(e), plough(e), plouw, from Old English plōh (“hide of land, ploughland”) and Old Norse plógr (“plough (the implement)”), both from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz, *plōguz (“plough”). Replaced Old English sulh (“plough, furrow”); see sullow.
plough.g: A device pulled through the ground in order to break it open into furrows for planting.

plower.g: One who plows; one who works land with a plow.

plowman.e: From Middle English plowman, ploghmon, plouȝman, equivalent to plow + man.
plowman.g: A man who plows land with a plow.

plowshare.e: From Middle English plowgh-schare, plowh schare, equivalent to plow + share. Eclipsed non-native Middle English culter (“ploughshare”), from Old English culter (“ploughshare, coulter, dagger”), borrowed from Latin culter (“knife, razor”).

pluck.e: From Middle English plucken, plukken, plockien, from Old English pluccian, ploccian (“to pluck, pull away, tear”), also Old English plyċċan ("to pluck, pull, snatch; pluck with desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *plukkōn, from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną, *plukkijaną (“to pluck”), of uncertain and disputed origin.
pluck.g: To pull something sharply; to pull something out

plumb.e: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.
plumb.g: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc., to indicate a vertical direction.

plummet.e: From Middle English plommet (“ball of lead, plumb of a bob-line”), recorded since 1382, from Old French plommet or plomet, the diminutive of plom, plum (“lead, sounding lead”), from Latin plumbum (“lead”).
plummet.g: A piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water; a plumb bob or a plumb line.

plump.e: From Middle English plump, plompe, a borrowing from Middle Dutch plomp or Middle Low German plump.
plump.g: Having a full and rounded shape; chubby, somewhat overweight.
A knot or cluster; a group; a crowd.

plunder.e: Recorded since 1632 during the Thirty Years War, native British use since the Cromwellian Civil War. Borrowed from German plündern (“to loot”), from Middle High German, from Middle Low German plunderen, from a noun originally meaning "household goods, bedding, clothing," of obscure ultimate origin.
plunder.g: To pillage, take or destroy all the goods of, by force (as in war); to raid, sack.

plunge.e: From Middle English plungen, ploungen, Anglo-Norman plungier, from Old French plongier, (Modern French plonger), from unattested Late Latin frequentative *plumbicō (“to throw a leaded line”), from plumbum (“lead”).
plunge.g: To thrust into liquid, or into any penetrable substance; to immerse.
To remove a blockage by suction.

plus.g: And; sum of the previous one and the following one.

ply.e: From Middle English pleit, plit, plite (“a fold, pleat, wrinkle; braid, strand in a braided cord, ply”), from Anglo-Norman pli, plei, pleit, and Middle French pli, ploy, ply (“a fold, pleat; joint in armour; situation, state”) (modern French pli (“a fold, pleat”)), from plier, ployer (“to bend, fold”), from Latin plicāre (“to bend, fold, roll up”).

From Middle English plīen, pli, plie (“to bend, fold, mould, shape; to be flexible; to be submissive, humble oneself; to compel someone to submit”), from Anglo-Norman plier, plaier, pleier, ploier, and Middle French plier, ployer (“to bend, fold; to be submissive; to compel someone to submit”) (modern French plier, ployer).
ply.g: To bend; to fold; to mould; (figuratively) to adapt, to modify; to change (a person's) mind, to cause (a person) to submit.
